question: What is the primary function of the hepatic portal vein?

options.A: Carrying synthesized bile salts away from the hepatocytes to the gallbladder
options.B: Draining systemic deoxygenated blood from the lower extremities to the heart
options.C: Delivering highly oxygenated blood directly from the left ventricle
options.D: Transporting nutrient-rich blood from the gastrointestinal tract to the liver

explanation: The hepatic portal vein uniquely channels venous blood laden with absorbed nutrients and toxins straight from the digestive organs into the hepatic circulation for processing. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h1)

question: A patient experiences a sharp decline in hepatic protein synthesis. Which clinical sign is most directly associated with this specific deficit?

options.A: Generalized peripheral edema due to decreased plasma oncotic pressure
options.B: Severe metabolic acidosis driven by unmanaged lactic acid accumulation
options.C: Persistent tachycardia resulting from an inability to clear circulating catecholamines
options.D: Marked hyperglycemia caused by total failure of hepatic glycogen storage

explanation: Hepatocytes synthesize albumin, the major plasma protein responsible for maintaining oncotic pressure; when synthesis drops, fluid leaks into the interstitial spaces, causing edema. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h1)

question: What is the primary pathological consequence of prolonged, chronic hepatic inflammation?

options.A: Rapid regeneration of functional hepatocytes replacing all scar tissue
options.B: Permanent dilation of the central hepatic veins and sinusoids
options.C: Deposition of fibrous connective tissue and structural scarring
options.D: Hypertrophy of the gallbladder leading to increased bile production

explanation: Persistent liver injury activates stellate cells, which lay down collagen and extracellular matrix proteins, leading to fibrosis and structural scarring over time. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h2)

question: Why do many patients with early-stage chronic liver disease remain asymptomatic for years?

options.A: The liver possesses extensive functional reserve and a high capacity for regeneration
options.B: Early pathological changes are strictly confined to the gallbladder and biliary tree
options.C: Peripheral tissues rapidly compensate for every metabolic failure of the liver
options.D: Hepatic nerve endings transmit pain signals only after complete organ failure

explanation: Because the liver has a large functional reserve, mild to moderate damage can be compensated for, delaying the appearance of noticeable clinical symptoms until advanced stages. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which viral hepatitis types are primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route?
explanation: Hepatitis A and E are enterically transmitted viruses spread mainly through ingestion of contaminated food and water, unlike the blood-borne strains B, C, and D. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary mechanism responsible for actual hepatocellular damage during viral hepatitis infections?

options.A: The host immune system attacking virus-infected hepatocytes
options.B: Ischemia resulting from viral blockage of the hepatic artery
options.C: Uncontrolled proliferation of Kupffer cells consuming healthy tissue
options.D: Direct toxic lysis of cells caused by viral replication alone

explanation: Much of the liver damage in viral hepatitis is immune-mediated, driven by cytotoxic T-cells and inflammatory responses targeting infected liver cells rather than direct viral toxicity. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h3)

question: What physical change characterizes hepatic cirrhosis at a microscopic level?

options.A: Complete disappearance of the central vein accompanied by massive fatty necrosis
options.B: Hypertrophy of healthy hepatocytes without any change in connective tissue
options.C: Dilation of the hepatic sinusoids with minimal alterations in the parenchyma
options.D: Replacement of normal architecture with fibrous scar tissue and regenerative nodules

explanation: Cirrhosis is defined histologically by widespread fibrosis and abnormal regenerative nodules that disrupt the entire architecture of the liver. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h4)

question: Why do patients with portal hypertension develop esophageal varices?

options.A: Esophageal tissue becomes inflamed due to chronic ingestion of spicy foods
options.B: Systemic arterial pressure rises significantly to compensate for poor cardiac output
options.C: Blood seeks alternative collateral pathways to bypass the high resistance in the liver
options.D: Hepatic synthesis of clotting factors triggers localized thrombosis in the neck

explanation: When intrahepatic blood flow is blocked by fibrosis, venous blood from the gut creates collateral channels through lower-resistance vessels like the esophageal veins, causing them to engorge. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h4)

question: What primary metabolic toxin is largely responsible for the development of hepatic encephalopathy?
explanation: Ammonia, generated by bacterial breakdown of proteins in the gut, fails to be converted into urea by the failing liver, crosses into the central nervous system, and induces neurotoxicity. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which clinical sign is considered a classic neurological indicator of early hepatic encephalopathy?
explanation: Asterixis, often called 'liver flap,' is an involuntary tremor observed when the patient extends the arms and dorsiflexes the wrists, signaling metabolic encephalopathy. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which blood test is considered more specific to hepatocellular injury because it is found predominantly in the liver?
explanation: While both AST and ALT rise with liver damage, ALT is heavily concentrated in hepatic tissue, making it a more specific marker for liver injury than AST. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of monitoring prothrombin time (PT/INR) in a client with severe liver disease?

options.A: To measure the exact concentration of circulating red blood cells
options.B: To quantify the amount of un-metabolized ammonia in the blood
options.C: To evaluate the liver's synthetic capacity for blood clotting factors
options.D: To detect active bacterial infections within the peritoneal cavity

explanation: The liver synthesizes most coagulation factors; therefore, a prolonged prothrombin time directly reflects impaired synthetic function and an elevated bleeding risk. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the mechanism of action of lactulose when treating hepatic encephalopathy?

options.A: It acts as a potent systemic antibiotic destroying all gastrointestinal flora
options.B: It directly stimulates hepatocytes to regenerate healthy functional tissue
options.C: It acidifies the intestinal tract, trapping ammonia in the gut for elimination
options.D: It binds to peripheral receptors in the brain to block circulating toxins

explanation: Lactulose lowers intestinal pH, converting soluble ammonia into poorly absorbed ammonium ions so they can be safely excreted in the stool. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h7)

question: Why are non-selective beta-blockers frequently prescribed for clients diagnosed with portal hypertension?

options.A: To stimulate renal filtration and rapidly eliminate excess ascites fluid
options.B: To suppress the immune system and stop autoimmune attacks on hepatocytes
options.C: To increase systemic blood pressure and improve overall cardiac output
options.D: To decrease portal venous pressure and prevent variceal hemorrhage

explanation: Non-selective beta-blockers reduce splanchnic vasoconstriction and heart rate, effectively lowering portal pressure and reducing the risk of fragile varices rupturing. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h7)

question: Which nursing intervention is essential when monitoring a client receiving diuretic therapy for ascites?

options.A: Checking deep tendon reflexes every two hours around the clock
options.B: Recording daily weights and exact abdominal girth measurements
options.C: Encouraging a high-sodium diet to prevent severe hyponatremia
options.D: Administering large intramuscular injections to ensure rapid absorption

explanation: Daily weights and abdominal girth measurements provide the most reliable objective data for tracking the accumulation or resolution of ascites fluid. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h8)

question: Which safety precaution is NOT appropriate for a client with advanced cirrhosis and a high risk of bleeding?

options.A: Using a very soft toothbrush for daily oral hygiene care
options.B: Monitoring all eliminated stool specimens for occult blood
options.C: Administering prescribed medications via the intramuscular route
options.D: Avoiding the use of sharp razors for shaving facial hair

explanation: Intramuscular injections should be avoided in clients with coagulopathy because the procedure can easily cause large hematomas and uncontrolled bleeding at the injection site. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h8)
